claims.text: High-temperature structural and chemical stability in high-entropy nanoalloys is governed by lattice-disorder-induced sluggish atomic diffusion.
Sluggish atomic diffusion inhibits phase segregation in high-entropy nanoalloys.
Sluggish atomic diffusion inhibits coarsening in high-entropy nanoalloys.
Multiple principal elements mixed in near-equiatomic ratios form a single-phase high-entropy nanoalloy structure.
High configurational entropy leads to lattice distortion.
Lattice distortion produces sluggish diffusion of the constituent atoms.
Lattice distortion creates energy barriers for atomic migration.
The migration barriers slow diffusion processes that would otherwise cause phase segregation, coarsening, and chemical degradation.
After identical high-temperature exposure, high-entropy nanoalloys will exhibit less grain growth than low-entropy binary or simpler nanoalloys.
After identical high-temperature exposure, high-entropy nanoalloys will exhibit less phase separation than low-entropy binary or simpler nanoalloys.
After identical high-temperature exposure, high-entropy nanoalloys will retain greater chemical homogeneity than low-entropy binary or simpler nanoalloys.
Low-entropy binary or ternary alloys have faster diffusion rates under the same high-temperature conditions.
The faster diffusion in low-entropy alloys leads to noticeable phase segregation and coarsening.
Using an inert or reducing atmosphere prevents oxidation effects during high-temperature exposure.
The prediction may cease to hold when composition moves outside the high-entropy regime.
Oxidizing environments can introduce degradation mechanisms beyond the proposed sluggish-diffusion mechanism.
Surface-energy effects or environmental passivation may provide additional stabilization.
